query: For high-entropy alloys used in thermal-insulation applications, what testable hypothesis could be made about an unspecified predictive approach for accurately identifying materials with low phonon thermal conductivity? The hypothesis should explain why the approach would work, predict its improvement over current predictions, define its applicability limits, identify supporting evidence, and specify a decisive experimental benchmark and outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A hybrid predictive model that integrates DFT-derived disorder descriptors—specifically local mass variance, force constant distribution, and phonon scattering rates—within a machine learning framework will reduce the mean absolute error in predicted lattice thermal conductivity of high-entropy alloys by at least 30% compared to traditional effective medium and simplified atomistic models.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloys (e.g., FeCoCrMnNi) possessing a disordered multi-element structure with significant atomic-scale fluctuations in both mass and force constants.
generation.intervention: Develop and apply a data-driven machine learning model trained on descriptors computed from DFT and lattice dynamics (capturing force constant fluctuations and local disorder) across a representative HEA compositional space.
generation.conditions: Measurements should be conducted under thermal-insulation operating conditions—spanning room temperature to elevated temperatures—where phonon transport is the dominant heat conduction mechanism. The model is applicable to alloys with 5–7 elemental compositions without phase separation or ordering effects.
generation.structural_mediator: Local atomic-scale disorder quantified by the variance in mass and force constants that mediates enhanced phonon scattering.
generation.mechanism: By incorporating detailed atomistic disorder parameters (derived from DFT) into an ML framework, the model more accurately accounts for the impact of force-constant fluctuations and chemical disorder on phonon scattering. This improved mechanistic representation enhances prediction accuracy of the low thermal conductivity regime.
generation.predicted_outcome: The predictive model will achieve a mean absolute error in lattice thermal conductivity predictions that is at least 30% lower than that of conventional effective medium theories within the designed compositional and temperature range.
generation.baseline: Predictions from traditional effective medium theories and simplified atomistic simulations that inadequately treat the complex disorder in HEAs.
generation.boundary: The approach is expected to be valid only for high-entropy alloys where chemical disorder predominates and is characterized by relatively uniform, albeit disordered, multi-element mixtures. Its performance may degrade for alloys exhibiting phase separation, ordering phenomena, or compositional regimes not represented in the training set.
generation.uncertainty: While preliminary evidence from DFT and experimental lattice dynamics studies supports the role of force-constant fluctuations in phonon scattering, the precise magnitude of improvement across different HEA systems and temperature regimes remains to be fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of benchmark high-entropy alloys spanning the target compositional space and measure their lattice thermal conductivity using inelastic neutron or X-ray scattering over a range of temperatures. Use the DFT+ML model to predict thermal conductivities for these alloys and compare the predictions with the experimental measurements.
measurements: Lattice thermal conductivity (via phonon lifetime and linewidth determinations)
Acoustic phonon dispersion and phonon linewidths
Calculation of mean absolute error against traditional models
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the model's predictions do not achieve at least a 30% reduction in mean absolute error relative to traditional prediction methods for more than 60% of the benchmark HEA samples, then the hypothesis—and hence the efficacy of the proposed integration of detailed disorder descriptors—is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Machine learning (ML) techniques have been actively utilized for various applications in recent years due to their superior prediction performance. However, as the applications expand vastly, they also have been required to meet the demand of high level of transparency and accountability due to their black-box framework. As a result, explainable ML methods have attracted a great deal of attention in order to further advance the reliability and applicability of ML-based approaches. Model explainability is also becoming increasingly important in the materials science domain as ML and artificial intelligence (AI)-driven algorithms are beginning to show success in simplifying various workflows. However, the idea of incorporating explainable ML methods into the current data-driven materials design and discovery workflow is still in its infancy. Unlike many other disciplines, materials science suffers from limited and sparse data. Incorporating interpretablility into the black-box ML models make it possible to explain the ML predictions with more confidence, especially when the models are trained using small and heterogeneous datasets. The difficulty of modeling phonon linewidths in random alloys comes from the complexity of taking into account the quoted three ingredients, i.e. atomic size, mass, and force-constant fluctuations. A simple analytical model, successfully used in mass disordered alloys, assumes phonon scattering from isolated defects and leads to the expression ΓFWHM = π/2(ℏω)2g(ℏω)〈ϵ2〉, where g(ℏω) is the GVDOS and ϵ represents the sum of all kinds of fluctuations contributions. Using this model, we find that the expected broadening from mass fluctuations in our HEA is negligibly small, at most 0.2 meV. Ascribing the whole observed linewidth to force-constant fluctuations, the global behavior is reproduced quite well along the [ζ00] direction using an average force-constant fluctuation ϵ = 〈ΔFij/Fij〉 ~ 20% (see Fig. 7). However, the agreement does not hold in all directions: the observed anisotropy then calls for more complex models. We therefore turn to the recent theoretical work of Mu et al.. As mentioned in the introduction, it is worth comparing the vibrational dynamics of our HEA to glasses and to crystalline materials with very large unit cells (CMAs), to identify similarities and differences and establish the place of HEAs with respect to these classes of materials. Specifically, as previously said, the low and weakly temperature dependent thermal conductivity in glasses has been associated to the existence of a strong phonon scattering due to the intrinsic disorder. Such regime, characterized by ΓFWHM ∝ (ℏω)4, has been reported in some glasses at energies corresponding to the deviation of the GVDOS from the Debye behavior and has lately been ascribed mostly to the force-constant disorder at a nanometric lengthscale. Interestingly, the same phenomenology arises in random matrix approaches, which model the vibrational properties of a glass through a random network of force-constants over a regular lattice, quite similarly to the case of our HEA,. It is thus important to check weather the same behavior can be found in our HEA, where force-constant fluctuations are the dominant phonon scattering source.

In conclusion, we have reported the first experimental investigation of the acoustic phonon dispersions in a High-Entropy Alloy, complemented by the GVDOS survey, at room and low temperature. FeCoCrMnNi is a 5-element random alloy, and, despite the inherent disorder, its phonon dynamics closely resemble that of the pure elements composing it and the corresponding binary alloys. More specifically, acoustic phonons disperse throughout the whole Brillouin zone up to energies between 20 and 30 meV, exhibiting an attenuation stronger than in simple elements, but of the same order of magnitude as in binary alloys. The whole attenuation behavior can be understood in terms of scattering from force-constant fluctuations, which have been estimated to amount to ~20% using a simple theoretical model, a value comparable with calculations of Mu and co-authors on binary and ternary alloys made of the same elements. If this is unexpected from Mu’s theory, which would predict increased force-constant fluctuations due to the larger variability of random environments of a given atomic pair, it explains recent experimental reports on comparable phonon lattice thermal conductivities in our HEA and FeNi

frame.system: High-entropy alloys used for thermal insulation, initially characterized by complex multi-element disordered structures where phonon scattering dominates heat transport.
frame.goal: Develop a predictive approach that accurately identifies HEAs with exceptionally low phonon thermal conductivity, thereby outperforming current models.
frame.limitation: Current predictive models inadequately capture the effects of chemical disorder and complex phonon scattering mechanisms in HEAs, leading to limited accuracy and poorly defined compositional applicability.

constraints: The hypothesis must explain the physical mechanism by which the approach improves prediction accuracy (e.g., by incorporating detailed atomistic disorder and phonon scattering models).
It should predict a quantifiable improvement over current predictions (for instance, a reduction in mean error or improved confidence intervals within a specific range of compositions).
It needs to clearly define the applicability limits (such as specific compositional ranges or thermal regimes where the approach remains valid).
The hypothesis should be supported by available indirect evidence (e.g., ab initio simulations or preliminary experimental data) and specify what evidence would be considered decisive.

A clearly defined experimental benchmark must be provided, along with a falsifiable outcome (for example, if measured phonon thermal conductivity in selected HEAs beyond the predicted limits deviates significantly from the model, the hypothesis would be falsified).
regime: Thermal-insulation operating conditions where phonon transport is dominant.
Likely relevant under both room temperature and elevated temperature conditions, where the influence of disorder on phonon scattering is pronounced.
prior_attempts: Existing models use effective medium theories or simplified phonon scattering approximations that do not fully capture the complexity of disorder in HEAs.

Early atomistic simulations and phenomenological models often fell short in predicting the extreme values of low thermal conductivity observed in some HEAs, leaving a gap in both understanding and predictive capability.

decision.trend: Early studies on HEAs focused on simplified effective medium theories or basic atomistic simulations that barely captured the full extent of chemical disorder and its effects on phonon scattering. Later, work such as that in PMC9726824 employed detailed lattice dynamics measurements and analyses to reveal the role of mass and force-constant fluctuations in attenuating propagating phonon modes, while subsequent studies like PMC9822225 combined density functional theory with on‐the‐fly machine learning to simulate thermal transport in high-entropy systems, demonstrating exceptionally low lattice thermal conductivity. Although these advances have improved our qualitative and even semi-quantitative understanding, existing models still struggle with accurate, predictive capabilities across the vast compositional space—particularly in reliably quantifying quantitative improvements and defining clear applicability limits.
decision.unsolved: The field still lacks a predictive methodology that can, in a general and systematically testable way, accurately forecast low phonon thermal conductivity in HEAs. In particular, no model has yet comprehensively integrated detailed atomistic disorder parameters to achieve a significant quantitative reduction in prediction error (e.g., >30% improvement over current models) and precisely delineate the compositional or thermal regimes where its predictions remain valid.
decision.lever: Develop a hybrid predictive model that couples DFT-derived disorder descriptors (e.g., local mass variance, force constant distribution, and phonon scattering rates) with machine learning regression techniques. Key parameters to optimize would include the weighting of atomic-scale disorder inputs and the selection of training datasets that span the relevant compositional ranges. The target is a model that reduces the mean absolute error in lattice thermal conductivity predictions by at least 30% compared to traditional effective medium theories.
decision.why: This strategy builds on recent trends where atomistic insights from DFT and lattice dynamics have already advanced our understanding of phonon behavior in disordered HEAs. By leveraging data-driven methods to integrate these complex descriptors, the approach directly addresses the gap in existing models. It also establishes quantifiable benchmarks—for example, if experimental measurements on benchmark HEAs deviate by more than a predefined tolerance from the model’s predictions, the hypothesis (and hence the model) would be falsified.
